title: A Different Kind of Loyalty
subtitle: After Always · Chapter 26 of 40
content:
Two days before the hearing, Snape received his formal notice to appear before the Wizengamot.

He read it in silence.

Then he corrected the date.

I looked over his shoulder.

“They wrote the twenty-third.”

“The hearing is the twenty-fourth.”

“You're being summoned by the government and your first response is proofreading.”

“The government should be more careful.”

“Terrifying priorities.”

He handed me the parchment.

His fingers were cold.

That was the only sign he was frightened.

The hearing would not be a criminal trial in the strict sense. Too much had already been established by testimony after the battle. Kingsley Shacklebolt had authorized a special review of Snape's wartime actions, teaching record, Death Eater involvement, and status under post-war amnesty provisions.

In other words, the Ministry had invented a room large enough to contain every contradiction and invited several dozen people to argue inside it.

Snape hated it.

“You do not have to attend,” he told me.

“I know.”

“You are not a witness unless called.”

“I know.”

“There will be press outside.”

“I know.”

“You should stay here.”

“No.”

His jaw tightened.

“You are not necessary.”

The word might once have hurt.

Now I heard the fear beneath it.

“I know that too.”

He looked at me.

“I am coming because I want to.”

His expression shifted.

“That is an insufficient reason.”

“For you?”

“For exposing yourself to spectacle.”

“I'm an adult.”

“A debatable condition.”

“Still coming.”

He turned away.

I let him.

Later that evening, I found him in the research lab staring at a row of potion bottles he had already labeled twice.

“You're nervous.”

“No.”

“You alphabetized.”

His head snapped toward the shelf.

I smiled.

“Domestic cupboard rules?”

“Leave.”

“No.”

He exhaled through his nose.

I took the stool beside him.

“What are you afraid they'll decide?”

His face closed.

I waited.

At last he said, “That nothing I did afterward matters.”

The answer surprised me.

I had expected imprisonment. Loss of wand rights. Public condemnation.

Not this.

“You think they'll reduce you to joining Voldemort.”

“Yes.”

“And the opposite?” I asked. “Are you afraid they'll decide what you did afterward erases everything before?”

Snape looked at me sharply.

“Yes.”

There it was.

The impossible position.

Condemnation felt false.

Absolution felt false.

He wanted a judgment complicated enough to hurt correctly.

“Maybe the hearing can't give you that,” I said.

His expression darkened.

“Then what is its purpose?”

“Legal status. Public record. Consequences.”

“Meaning?”

“Meaning maybe the Ministry is bad at souls.”

A pause.

Then, unexpectedly, Snape laughed.

“That may be the first intelligent thing you have said all month.”

“I'm putting it in the report.”

“Please do.”

We sat in silence.

I looked at his left forearm. The Mark was hidden under his sleeve.

“Lucius asked you not to testify against him.”

“Yes.”

“Are you going to?”

“Yes.”

“Even if it hurts his case badly?”

“Yes.”

“Were you loyal to him once?”

Snape's mouth tightened.

“I thought so.”

“What changed?”

“Everything.”

“That is vague.”

“You ask questions with answers too large for the room.”

“Try.”

He looked down at his hands.

“I once thought loyalty meant remaining,” he said. “Staying beside people. Protecting secrets. Refusing betrayal.”

I listened.

“It took me an embarrassing amount of time to understand that loyalty to a person can become disloyalty to every principle one claims to possess.”

“That sounds like Dumbledore.”

His eyes narrowed.

“It does not.”

“It does a little.”

“Retract it.”

“No.”

His mouth twitched.

“What does loyalty mean now?” I asked.

Snape was quiet.

“Telling the truth when silence would be kinder to myself.”

That landed heavily.

“That's what the hearing is?”

“Partly.”

“And Lucius?”

“Yes.”

“And me?”

The question escaped.

Snape went still.

I had not meant to place myself beside war and testimony.

Too late.

He turned toward me fully.

“What about you?”

“What does loyalty look like with me?”

His face changed in small ways.

Tension at the mouth.

Thought behind the eyes.

Fear, perhaps.

Then he held out his hand.

I placed mine in it.

“This,” he said.

I waited.

“When I am angry, I do not get to injure you and call it honesty.”

His thumb moved across my knuckles.

“When I am afraid, I do not get to decide for you what you should know.”

I breathed carefully.

“When you say no, I stop.”

My throat tightened.

“When you choose to leave a room, I do not make leaving a punishment.”

That one hurt in a way he probably did not know.

“And when you choose to stay?” I asked.

His grip tightened.

“I attempt to believe you.”

That was Severus Snape's version of romance.

Not forever.

Not destiny.

An attempt to believe a choice offered freely.

I lifted his hand and pressed my mouth to his knuckles.

He froze.

The contact was brief.

When I lowered his hand, his expression had gone completely unguarded.

“Was that all right?” I asked.

“Yes.”

His voice was rough.

“Do you want me to do it again?”

A pause.

“Yes.”

I did.

This time his eyes closed.

The moment felt more intimate than a kiss might have.

Perhaps because it was not stolen by momentum.

It was asked.

Answered.

Repeated.

Outside, snow tapped softly against the narrow windows.

The hearing waited two days away.

For that evening, loyalty meant nothing grander than staying beside him while he reorganized bottles that did not need reorganizing.

When I left, they were alphabetical.

I did not mention it.\n\nI reached the door before he spoke again.\n\n“Jasper.”\n\nI turned.\n\nSnape had not moved from the worktable. One hand rested beside the newly alphabetized bottles, fingers spread against the wood as if he needed the contact to keep the room still.\n\n“Yes?”\n\nHis eyes went to the door, then back to me.\n\n“If tomorrow becomes unpleasant—”\n\n“It will.”\n\nHis expression sharpened. “I had intended to finish the sentence.”\n\n“Sorry. Continue your prophecy.”\n\n“If tomorrow becomes unpleasant,” he repeated, “you are not required to remain.”\n\nThe careful phrasing told me he had been thinking about it for a while. Not whether I would come. Whether I would leave once the room became cruel.\n\nI leaned one shoulder against the doorframe. “Are you asking me to leave?”\n\n“No.”\n\n“Are you telling me to?”\n\n“No.”\n\n“Then what are you doing?”\n\nHis mouth tightened.\n\n“Providing an exit.”\n\nThe answer made something in my chest ache.\n\nI crossed back to the table. “You know what is interesting about exits?”\n\n“I am certain you intend to tell me.”\n\n“They work in both directions.”\n\nHe frowned.\n\n“If I need to leave, I can leave,” I said. “If you need five minutes without me, tell me. If you want me there, say that too. You do not have to disguise every request as permission for someone else to abandon you.”\n\nThe silence afterward was so complete I could hear one of the cooling charms click off inside the cabinet.\n\nSnape looked down at the labels.\n\n“That was an unnecessarily theatrical interpretation.”\n\n“Was it wrong?”\n\nHis jaw worked.\n\n“No.”\n\nThe word was quiet.\n\nI stayed beside the table instead of reaching for him. He had taught me enough by then to know that care offered too quickly could feel like a trap.\n\nAfter a while he said, “I would prefer you attend.”\n\nThere it was. Not a command. Not a warning. A preference, stated plainly enough to be vulnerable.\n\n“I will.”\n\n“You may regret that decision.”\n\n“I regret most decisions eventually. It keeps me humble.”\n\n“You have never been humble.”\n\n“Then it keeps me entertained.”\n\nHis mouth twitched.\n\nI picked up the summons again. “Twenty-fourth.”\n\n“Yes.”\n\n“Nine in the morning.”\n\n“Yes.”\n\n“Formal robes?”\n\n“Unfortunately.”\n\n“Do I get to criticize them?”\n\n“No.”\n\n“Can I think criticisms very loudly?”\n\n“I suspect you do most things loudly.”\n\n“Rude.”\n\n“Accurate.”\n\nThe ease of the exchange did not erase the hearing. It only made fear share the room with something else.\n\nWhen I finally left, Snape walked me as far as the dungeon stairs. He did not claim he happened to be going that direction. Progress had limits, apparently.\n\nAt the first landing I looked back.\n\nHe was still there.\n\n“Tomorrow,” I said.\n\nSnape inclined his head. “Tomorrow.”\n\nNeither of us called that loyalty.\n\nWe did not need to.

alternate compact emotional beats with fuller reflective paragraphs
let dialogue carry relationship pressure while narration carries interior consequence
use humor and ordinary practical actions to make vulnerable scenes feel lived-in rather than staged
favor character-specific reactions and small remembered details over generic declarations
allow grief, identity, survival, belonging, home, change, vulnerability, care, and autonomy to recur as thematic pressure
end scenes or chapters on an emotional consequence, changed understanding, concrete image, callback, or forward pull
preserve first-person immediacy and avoid omniscient knowledge outside Jasper's perception
use semicolons selectively for linked thoughts rather than mechanically
dialogue_fingerprint: continuous dialogue should sound conversational rather than like alternating speeches
interrupt dialogue with gestures, environment, hesitation, humor, and internal reaction
let characters dodge, misunderstand, tease, repair, and return to earlier wording
do not make every character equally eloquent, equally dominant, or equally emotionally transparent

attraction should not erase plot, outside obligations, individual goals, or conflict
vulnerability is strongest when it changes later behavior
after an intense/private interlude, resume with reconnection, humor, care, consequences, memory updates, and the next plot beat rather than treating intimacy as a reset
